Content: Triangles are a key pillar of geometry and spatial analysis. Because triangles are the only polygon that cannot deform without altering the length of its sides, they are foundational for structural stability in the real world,. Understanding triangle theorems is what allows engineers to design reliable bridges and surveyors to map out property boundaries. On the SAT exam, triangles and their unique properties are a big component within the Geometry and Trigonometry category. Certain SAT problems present models where triangles are nested inside circles or combined to form complex polygons, so it's useful to be able to apply core geometric rules to dismantle multi-step problems. Understanding triangle theorems and relationships within a right triangle provides a robust toolkit to instantly simplify complex visual layouts and identify a path to the solution.

The most fundamental rule governing any three-sided figure is the triangle sum theorem. This theorem states that the interior angles of any triangle in a flat plane will always add up to exactly `180°`, no matter how it's shaped. On the SAT exam, this theorem means that knowing any two angles in a triangle allows the third to be found simply by subtracting the other two values from `180`. Another tool for finding a triangle's missing angles is the Exterior Angle Theorem. This theorem states that the measure of an exterior angle of a triangle is exactly equal to the sum of the two angles inside the triangle that are not touching the exterior angle. When working on SAT problems in the Geometry and Trigonometry category, these rules let us “angle chase” by using a known values in a triangle to unlock other angles in the triangle or even angles within neighboring shapes.

When a triangle contains a perfect `90°` angle, it becomes a right triangle - which has its own special set of structural rules. The two sides that meet to form the right angle are called the legs and the third side, directly opposite the `90°` angle, is the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse is unique because it is always the absolute longest side of a right triangle. The legs and the hypotenuse balance one another, forming a relationship known as the Pythagorean Theorem. This theorem states that the sum of the squares of the lengths of the legs is equal to the square of the length of the hypotenuse - described by the equation `a^2+b^2=c^2`. In this relationship, `a` and `b` represent the lengths of either legs, while `c` must always represent the length of the hypotenuse. Applying the Pythagorean theorem allows us to calculate a missing side of any right triangle as long as the other two side lengths are known. Even further, there are some common combinations of side lengths called Pythagorean triples. Recognizing these common side ratios, like $3:4:5$ and $5:12:13$ (as well as their multiples), makes it possible to identify missing side lengths without the need to write out equations and perform calculations.

Special right triangles — specifically the `45°-45°-90°` and `30°-60°-90°` triangles — are another invaluable shortcut for finding missing side lengths on the SAT exam. Any triangles formed by the same angles will always maintain a fixed, predictable ratio between their side lengths. While the Pythagorean theorem requires two known sides to find a missing one, special triangles allow you to identify all side lengths if given just one. In an isosceles `45°-45°-90°` triangle, the side lengths scale according to the ratio `x:x:xsqrt2` where hypotenuse is always the length of a leg multiplied by `sqrt2`. In a `30°-60°-90°` triangle, the sides compare to each other with the ratio `x:xsqrt3:2x` where `x` is the short leg (opposite the `30°` angle), `xsqrt3` is the long leg (opposite the `60°` angle), and `2x` is the hypotenuse.

Memorizing these theorems and patterns is critical for working through geometric puzzles in certain SAT problems. Details about a triangle may be buried inside word problems about square diagonals or equilateral triangles, so recognizing even just one angle within a triangle directs us toward the right method to solve for a missing value. The best strategy when facing triangle problems on the SAT is to actively look for right angles and special instances where angles or side lengths take on familiar values with a known pattern.
